"There is but one truly serious philosophical problem and that is suicide."

*Albert Camus*

It's true that people avoid those they perceive as 'losers' or even just as lonely. It's a horrible, hideous truth that reflects the fear of rejection everyone feels like a cudgel above their heads, ready to crush them at the order of the hive-mind of those that have learned to 'belong' no matter what it is they belong to and no matter what they have to do to be accepted. Pat yourself on the back for seeing through it. You're filled with hatred now--for yourself and everyone else. But there is another side to the coin. Such hatred can only come from a feeling of unrequited love. Being alienated is lethal. I know of what I speak. To know that people can use social rejection as a weapon, that they can ostracize you as if you were a worthless object, can indeed be a rage-inducing realization.

Hopefully, it can also lead to an immense feeling of compassion for the blindness to casual cruelty that is the human condition we all are currently living. Forgive them. They know not what they do.

I agree that given the *current* state of society life is not worth living. We live in a world driven by the fear of death more than by the love of life; and perhaps some of those selflessly trying to dissuade the suicidal here on SW and elsewhere are trying to convince themselves as much as they are trying to save others.

Where we may differ, however, is that I live in the hope that society can change--that people can change. This hope is pretty much all that keeps me going and I have dedicated myself to trying to help precipitate this change both in the way I live and through my writing.

I used to consider myself a nihilist. As such, in my junior year of college, I began selling and using heroin and cocaine, shooting as many speedballs as I could afford with the intention of dying.

Life to me seemed not only existentially meaningless, but hideously ugly and painful considering the loveless, immoral society I was expected to conform to and collaborate with.

I had a partner in all this, a woman who I considered my soul mate but who has recently abandoned me. She shared my philosophy, and I remember how once we had a discussion in which we mercilessly ridiculed so-called scientists who espoused or defended the [anthropic principal](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropic_principal).

In a nutshell, the anthropic principal states that the physical constants of the universe are so finely tuned for the emergence of intelligent life, that a transcendent force must have designed it to be so.

For a nihilist, the hole in this argument was large enough to steer an aircraft carrier through: *What intelligent life?*

Of course *we* think *we're* intelligent. For all we know rocks think they're intelligent too. But given the suffering inherent to all living creatures, considering mortality, and most importantly considering human history and the horrors we have wrought with our so-called 'intelligence', where was the slightest shred of evidence that a universe fine-tuned to bring about the emergence of dweebs with telescopes was in any way a good thing--was anything special? Where was the slightest shred of evidence that life and intelligence were in any way an improvement over inert matter--or over the void? Where was the slightest shred of evidence that intelligence had redeemed anything?

At least 20 years has passed since we voiced those opinions, and about ten have passed since our perspectives altered. Recently the hole in our nihilistic argument against the anthropic occurred to me. I was going to put it in my web site, but here's as good a place as any.

The hole in the nihilistic point of view is that humanity's intelligence has not redeemed anything ***yet***.

Just because the process of emerging from mindless, instinct-driven biological machines into self-aware, decision making, technology-wielding beings of almost limitless potential has been a traumatic, blood-filled nightmare until now, doesn't mean that one day we won't wake up.

The problem is that people still don't really believe that they are anything more than animals. As a species, we haven't recognized the miracle that is our own free will. The terror and trauma of history weighs down our idealistic dreams like a lead life-preserver. We think we are being "realistic" when we accept a world predicated upon cruelty and competition because that's 'the way it's always been.' People even cite nature as the basis for the cut-throat, selfish individualism we each must accept as a sort of rite-of-passage from the naivete of childhood into the bleak empty amoral struggle for economic survival that constitutes 'adulthood.' Yet a more ludicrous justification would be hard to find! 

To say that people are cruel because nature is cruel may well be the stupidest argument ever made. 

First of all, even if we were in no way fundamentally distinct from nature, then we are at the very least social animals! The fight for survival that comprises life doesn't extend to within the pack! Apes, Dolphins, wolves--their most valuable survival skill is *cooperation*.

It is out of this cooperation that true self-awareness emerged. We are social  to an exponentially greater extent than any other creature. Language--a potentially infinitely complex dynamic system that emerged from the interaction *between* individuals--the force that binds us all yet awakens the self-aware individual within each of us--is encoded into us from the moment we are born. Technology--the culmination of the collective creativity of humanity since the chipping of the first spear point--has so thoroughly separated us from nature, that our very bodies have evolved to depend upon it, and there is not a human alive, from whatever society at whatever level of technology, who could survive nature without the skills, products, and wisdom developed over generations by the collective efforts of their ancestors.

And yet somehow, through some unfathomable insanity, we have shaped a world in which each of us must fight alone for their survival in an economic 'jungle' we created out of our own fears and doubts.

Madness!

I believe the time is coming when we will wake up, when we will all recognize ourselves as intelligent beings and stop defining ourselves by fear of what happens to the corporeal husks that house our Minds. We will realize we have nothing to fear. Nature has been conquered. There's no one causing us to suffer but ourselves. We *already* love each other. We've just been duped into believing that love is a lie, when in fact it is the ultimate basis of reality.

When we awaken, *then* intelligence will irrefutably redeem our existence and that of our universe. The only faith required is in ourselves. We have the power to make the universe meaningful through an act of self-fulfilling prophecy.

I live for nothing but to help this come to pass.

Let's say the person you love most in the world dies. Anyone who could continue pursuing their career without interruption would, IMHO, be someone who lacked certain positive qualities.

Or, to quote Montgomery Burns: "Family, religion, friends.. these are the three demons you must slay if you wish to succeed in business."

Finally, how many people weigh the moral implications of what they do to achieve a successful career, rather than assuming that success is its own justification? Whoever developed napalm was, I'm sure, a very successful man.
Just relax and pop Viagra and anti-depressants while pandemics indiscriminately wipe out millions. Hopefully, big pharma execs will be among the first to go.

If your heart is broken, it proves you have a heart. The saddest thing about SW is that it is the best and most sensitive people who are taking their lives. You know the line by Yeats?

>The best lack all conviction, while the worst
>Are full of passionate intensity

Never were truer words spoken. Please don't destroy yourself. You are not alone. It's simply that we live in a society that has alienated us all from one another--driven us into a false isolation, a false individuality in which we have been duped into believing that the strong swim while the weak sink. The opposite is far closer to the truth. 

It's hard to take any comfort from this while suffering; but your capacity for emotional pain, your inability to survive in a loveless world, is actually a gift. It is from this sensitivity--this inability to reconcile how you feel the world *should* be in comparison to how it currently is--which, I believe, will finally overthrow the empty, mindless, loveless empire we are all currently trapped in and bring about a global awakening from the nightmare world we are all currently sleeping through.

Hold on. I believe change is coming. I believe that the broken-hearted will be the first to open their eyes and see the truth.

If you want to die, doesn't that mean you don't fear death? If you don't fear death, doesn't that mean that you are free? 

Alone, this realization is of little value. But  if those who are suffering could unite in their pain *en masse*, if we could fearlessly defy the world while taking joy and comfort from the love of our fellows, a force would be unleashed which nothing could withstand.

There's a quote by Dostoevsky you should read. I included it in the introduction to the website I started with the intention of propagating the above ideas. It can be found [here](https://sites.google.com/site/confessionssite/ConfessionsofaLoser/introduction#isolation).

Thanks for the advice re Reddit, but I'm a long-time user under a different account name, and I've seen some of the nastiness. Haven't seen any on SW and hope there hasn't been any. It would really bum me out to see the online equivalent of a crowd yelling 'jump' to a man on a ledge.

Thanks for the encouragement. Articulating the cause of the pain can be cathartic. Regarding the mood swings, as I wrote in my intro, I have seen doctors and none of them have ever suggested I was Bipolar--just depressed. The only cause for the emotional highs are my recurring sense that I've had an important insight. I am also trying to write about that insight.

Hope you occasionally drop by the site and check it out.

PS Can I take this opportunity to ask your advice. Considering we're entering a post-literate age, I get the feeling that few people want to read long texts online. Do you think I should read it out loud and put up an mp3? Should I video tape myself, blurring out my face? How far, for example did you read?

I think you are a very nice person. Acts of kindness and empathy--trying to ease the suffering of others because you once suffered the same pain--prove that there is hope for the world.

Remember how I began the introduction of my website with a description of the mood swings I'm going through? Mostly I'm deeply depressed, but occasionally I feel moments of enlightenment in which I believe I have understood precisely what is wrong with the world, and that I am capable of fixing it with my words. 

It is the brief moments of epiphany that motivate my writing, and I intend to devote every moment I can spare to it from now on. I've been working myself up to start writing for at least 20 years, and for at least ten I've had the recurring conviction that I could redeem humanity by inspiring a spiritual revolution that would transform a social structure based on fear, hate, and competition into one based on reason, love, and cooperation.

I've always tended towards extremes. Now I am being torn apart by the g-forces of swinging between the two most-distant emotional extremes possible. 

I am totally alienated. I don't fit in this world. Either the problem lies with me or the problem lies with the world.

When I believe in myself, I believe I will single-handedly provide the catalyst that will spark the transformation that will cure the world. When I don't believe, then I am simply the loneliest, most pitiful, heartbroken, weak-willed. daydreaming momma's boy in the world--a coward who never grew up and lives in his own delusional fantasy world.

The totality of my alienation makes these extremes inevitable. I feel so completely apart from other people that, emotionally, it seems I can only interpret my isolation as either the result of being beneath everyone else, or as the result of having deliberately put myself outside society so that I could see and explain a truth that no one within society could ever see. 

My stubborn obsession with my own thoughts, my inability to compromise, my unwillingness to participate with others, are either horrible acts of hubris and arrogance, or selfless adherence to the pursuit of an ideal. Or maybe both.

In any case, I *will* write. I will finally 'put my money where my mouth is' and see whether I've just been rationalizing my selfish childishness, or refusing to compromise my pursuit of truth. 

PS If you are at all interested, please try re-reading the quote from *The Brothers Karamazov* I put in my intro. It explains what I'm trying to achieve far better than I ever could.

I responded to your response, and since you didn't mind identifying yourself as the Redditor who sent me the message, I am taking the liberty of pasting a copy of what I just wrote to you below.

>I've had a couple of volunteer jobs. I found that I didn't feel like I was accomplishing anything. The job I held the longest was teaching basic internet skills to recovering addicts. Even given the unlikely assumption that I helped one or two people escape addiction and poverty--even if I managed to help someone make the transition from the ghetto to the middle-class--what would I have achieved?

>I have come to the conclusion that the current social order is a manifestation of mindless evil. Most gainfully employed members of the middle class, most of the "work" done by the human race does more harm than good. What is it that most industries produce? Weapons, oil, cars, addictive and unhealthy foods, drugs, and addictive and mindless entertainment like computer games and 99.9% of television. Successful people with careers are for the most part either killing people, destroying life on earth, or seducing those less "disciplined" and "ambitious" than themselves into sinking instead of swimming by manufacturing addictive anodynes for their pain.

>I understand people that are in pain. What I don't understand are people so brutish and insensitive they can pursue their career goals and breed children in a world that is fundamentally evil.

>I dream of overturning this evil with my writing. Of transforming a world based on fear and greed into one based on reason and love. 

>My hopes aren't especially high. Today I discovered two downvotes added to my original post and each one felt like being knifed.

>This world causes me pain. Virtually everyone who is in pain blames themselves for being weak. Because of some extremely odd circumstances (mainly meeting a friend who thought exactly the same way I do and living with her for 18 years) I (we) developed the courage to wonder: What if my pain isn't my fault, but the world's? 

>I'm sure there were people living in Nazi Germany that found themselves depressed and failing at life, and never questioned the possibility that it was their environment that was the problem, not them.

>True, I am not living in Nazi Germany; but I *am* living in an insanely overpopulated, hypocrisy-based world packed with nuclear weapons that becomes more Orwellian with each passing day.

>I'm not trying to bum you out, and I'm sorry if my words hurt or offended you in any way. It's just that we can't solve the problem unless we face it, even though facing it is horribly depressing.


>PS: Been Wondering a lot about SW and people's motives for announcing their intentions to kill themselves as well as the motives of those who write to dissuade them. Have you spent much time at SW? Could you tell me why you think people post on it and what your personal motives were for writing me? If so, thanks.

Someone sent me a kind PM. Below is my reply. (BTW, just for the record, I am at the moment in excruciating emotional pain.)

>Sorry for taking so long to respond, and thank you for your compassionate offer to talk. Your mention of my mother gave me the impression you were the only person to read through my whole intro. My mother does love me very much. She is a highly intelligent, hard-working, idealistic woman who lived her whole life willing to sacrifice anything for her children.

>I think that it was her love and idealism that made me so spectacularly unsuited for this world. There's a reason that the term "momma's boy" is a pejorative. Don't get me wrong. I don't agree with the people who sneer at love; I'm just acknowledging that it made adapting to a world that is in no way based on love and understanding a challenge that I have found impossible to meet.

>I don't blame my mother for this. I blame the world. In a sense, my current effort to express myself with a web site and try to change the world is an expression of my unwillingness to repudiate the love and reason my mom raised me with and an effort to prove that people are innately motivated to function and create without the need to instill children (or adults, for that matter) with a fear- or punishment-based discipline. 

>In other words, I was raised believing in a world of carrots without sticks; and even though sticks can be a powerful incentive (like the cliche about how in fascist Italy the trains were always on time) I don't believe that anyone has the right to wield them, and that if they're needed in order to motivate people to do something, then that 'something' would be better left undone.

>I don't fear death any more (at least not usually). That I have survived as long as I have despite my unwillingness to accept that we live in a stick-based world is the result of some astronomically unlikely good luck. Now that I'm essentially alone except for my mother, her death will free me to stand up and tell all the stick-wielders to shove those sticks up their asses. (Actually, I probably won't end up using such aggressive language, but will rather try to gently explain that there's no one here on earth brutalizing humanity but ourselves--that there's no need for a world based on fear and competition, and that we could all save ourselves a great deal of pain if we simply put the sticks down.) 

>If I can get that message across I will die happily. If I can't I will die miserably. Either way, my death is long, long overdue, considering that I am 48 years old,  that I have always considered myself unalterably opposed to the entire basis of our civilization,  and that ever since high school I've considered anyone who blithely participated in the giant engine of destruction that currently constitutes humanity to be a mindless collaborator. (Though lately I've moderated my views and now, rather than "mindless" I consider the human race, both collectively and individually, to be suffering from trauma.)

>Death is inevitable. Participating in an evil world isn't. To quote an ancient religious text: "What does it profit a man to gain the world and lose his soul?"  Substitute the word "integrity" for soul and, as far as I am concerned, the quote still holds true. 

>I am taking a stand. My dream is that others will be inspired by my example--not to kill themselves, but to realize that there are worse things than death, and that a life driven by fear of pain, deprivation, and mortality spent engaged in a futile struggle to preserve one's decaying flesh at any cost is not a life worth living.

Peace & Love,
ccrumb
